topics.title: Eastern Slavs and the formation of the Old Russian state
topics.content:
Origin and settlement of the Eastern Slavs

The Eastern Slavs separated from the common Slavic community in the 6th–7th centuries. They occupied a vast territory of Eastern Europe from Lake Ilmen in the north to the Black Sea steppes in the south, from the Carpathian Mountains in the west to the Volga River in the east. Main tribal unions: Polans (Kyiv), Drevlyans, Severians, Krivichs, Vyatichs, Ilmen Slavs (Novgorod), and others.

Occupations and social structure
  • Agriculture: slash-and-burn and shifting cultivation, later arable farming (plough, wooden plough).
  • Animal husbandry: cattle, pigs, horses.
  • Crafts: hunting, fishing, beekeeping (collection of wild honey).
  • Handicrafts and trade: growth of cities (Kyiv, Novgorod, Smolensk), the trade route "from the Varangians to the Greeks".

Social structure – clan community, later transforming into a neighbouring (territorial) community. Major issues were decided at the veche – a popular assembly.

Beliefs

Paganism: worship of the forces of nature, ancestor cult. Pantheon of gods: Perun (god of thunder and war), Veles (god of cattle), Dazhbog (sun deity), Svarog (god of sky and fire), and others.

Prerequisites for state formation
  • Economic development, emergence of surpluses and social inequality.
  • Growth of cities and trade.
  • External danger – raids by the Varangians (Scandinavians) and Khazars.
  • Tribal unions needed unification for defence and trade.
The calling of the Varangians (862) and the beginning of statehood

According to the Primary Chronicle, the Ilmen Slavs and neighbouring tribes invited the Varangian prince Rurik with his brothers to end internal strife. Rurik settled in Novgorod. The debate between Normanists and anti-Normanists about the role of the Varangians continues to this day.

Unification of Novgorod and Kyiv

In 882, Rurik's successor – Prince Oleg – captured Kyiv, killing Askold and Dir who ruled there. Thus a single state – Kyivan Rus – was formed, with its capital in Kyiv.

topics.title: Kyivan Rus in the 10th – early 12th centuries
topics.content:
Reign of the first princes
  • Oleg (882–912): continued the unification of the Eastern Slavic tribes, led successful campaigns against Byzantium, concluded favourable trade treaties.
  • Igor (912–945): suppressed tribal uprisings, was killed while collecting tribute from the Drevlyans.
  • Olga (945–964): avenged her husband's death, carried out tax reform – established fixed tribute amounts (uroki) and collection points (pogosty). The first ruler of Rus to adopt Christianity (in Constantinople).
  • Svyatoslav (964–972): famous for his military campaigns, destroyed the Khazar Khaganate, fought in Bulgaria and against Byzantium. Killed by the Pechenegs.
Vladimir I the Great (980–1015)
  • Attempt to create a unified pagan pantheon.
  • Choice of faith and the Baptism of Rus (988) – adoption of Christianity according to the Eastern (Byzantine) rite. Significance: strengthening of princely power, development of culture and writing, expansion of international ties.
  • Strengthening of borders, construction of cities.
Yaroslav the Wise (1019–1054)

The heyday of Kyivan Rus. Main deeds:

  • Compilation of the first written code of laws – "Russkaya Pravda" (Yaroslav's Truth).
  • Dynastic marriages with the ruling houses of Europe (his daughters were married to the kings of Norway, Hungary, and France).
  • Construction of St. Sophia Cathedral in Kyiv.
  • Strengthening the international authority of Rus.

topics.title: Feudal fragmentation in Rus (12th – 13th centuries)
topics.content:
Causes of fragmentation
  • Growth of votchina landownership (boyars and local princes strengthened their economic independence).
  • Strengthening of individual city centres.
  • Decline of the trade route "from the Varangians to the Greeks".
  • Lack of a clear succession order (the lateral system led to internecine wars).
Lyubech Congress (1097)

The princes agreed: "everyone shall keep his own patrimony", which consolidated the division of lands and initiated political fragmentation.

Largest principalities and lands
  • Vladimir-Suzdal Principality (north‑east) – princes Yuri Dolgoruky, Andrei Bogolyubsky, Vsevolod the Big Nest. Foundation of Moscow (1147).
  • Galicia-Volhynia Principality (south‑west) – powerful boyars, Prince Daniel of Galicia.
  • Novgorod Republic – veche, posadnik, the prince was invited with limited functions.
Consequences of fragmentation
  • Positive: flourishing of cities, culture, development of local crafts and trade.
  • Negative: weakening of military power, disunity in the face of external threats.

topics.title: Mongol invasion and establishment of the yoke (1237–1240)
topics.content:
Mongol Empire and campaigns

At the beginning of the 13th century, Genghis Khan united the Mongol tribes and created a powerful army. His grandson Batu led the campaign to the West.

Battle of the Kalka River (1223)

The first clash of Russian princes with the Mongols. The united Rus‑Cuman army was defeated due to lack of coordination.

Batu's invasion (1237–1240)
  • 1237–1238 – devastation of the Ryazan and Vladimir principalities, battle on the Sit River (Vladimir prince Yuri Vsevolodovich was killed).
  • 1239–1240 – campaign against Southern Rus: capture of Chernigov, Pereyaslavl, Kyiv (1240).
Reasons for the defeat of the Russian principalities
  • Fragmentation and lack of unified command.
  • Numerical and tactical superiority of the Mongol army (discipline, cavalry, siege engines).
Establishment of the Horde yoke

The system of dependence of Rus on the Golden Horde:

  • Princes received a yarlyk (patent) to rule.
  • Regular payment of tribute (vykhod).
  • Oversight by baskaks – the Khan's representatives.
Consequences
  • Economic decline, destruction of cities.
  • Isolation from Western Europe.
  • Change of the political system: strengthening of the princes' autocratic power.
  • Influence on culture (Asian elements).
Alexander Nevsky (prince of Novgorod, Vladimir)

Policy: struggle against Western aggression (Battle of the Neva 1240, Battle on the Ice 1242) and cooperation with the Horde (suppression of uprisings, obtaining yarlyks) – a pragmatic choice for the survival of Rus.

topics.title: Rise of Moscow and unification of Russian lands (14th – 15th centuries)
topics.content:
Reasons for the rise of Moscow
  • Favourable geographical position (intersection of trade routes, distance from the Horde, forests protected from raids).
  • Support of the Russian Orthodox Church (Metropolitan Peter moved the see to Moscow).
  • Flexible policy of Moscow princes toward the Horde and other principalities.
The first Moscow princes
  • Ivan Kalita (1325–1340): received the yarlyk for the grand princely throne, expanded the territory, suppressed the Tver uprising, attracted the metropolitan to Moscow.
  • Dmitry Donskoy (1359–1389): strengthened Moscow, defeated the Horde at the Kulikovo Field (1380). Significance of the battle – growth of national consciousness, Moscow became the leader. In 1382 – Tokhtamysh's raid, burning of Moscow, but Moscow's role was already undeniable.
Feudal war of the second quarter of the 15th century

Struggle for power between Vasily II (the Blind) and his uncle Yuri Dmitrievich, and then with his cousins. Ended with Vasily II's victory, which strengthened autocracy.

Ivan III (1462–1505) – "Sovereign of All Rus"
  • Annexation of Novgorod (1478) and Tver (1485).
  • Great Stand on the Ugra River (1480): final overthrow of the Horde yoke.
  • Adoption of the Sudebnik of 1497 – a unified code of laws, restricting peasant movement (St. George's Day, 26 November).
  • Construction of the Moscow Kremlin, formation of the idea "Moscow – the Third Rome".

topics.title: Russia in the 16th century. Ivan the Terrible.
topics.content:
Vasily III (1505–1533)

Completion of the unification of Russian lands: annexation of Pskov (1510), Smolensk (1514), Ryazan (1521).

Regency of Elena Glinskaya and boyar rule

After the death of Vasily III, the young Ivan IV was ruled by his mother Elena Glinskaya, then by boyar factions, which weakened central authority.

Ivan IV the Terrible (1533–1584)
  • 1547 – crowning as tsar, adoption of the title "tsar".
Reforms of the Chosen Council (1549–1560)
  • New Sudebnik of 1550.
  • Convocation of Zemsky Sobors (assemblies of the land).
  • Military reform: creation of the streltsy army, the "chosen thousand".
  • Guba and zemstvo reforms (local self‑government).
  • Stoglavy Council (1551) – unification of church rites.
Foreign policy
  • Annexation of Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan (1556) – access to the Volga, elimination of fragments of the Horde.
  • Yermak's campaign and the beginning of the conquest of Siberia (1581–1585).
  • Livonian War (1558–1583) for access to the Baltic – defeat, loss of fortresses.
Oprichnina (1565–1572)
  • Division of the country into the zemshchina and the oprichnina with a special army.
  • Mass terror against the boyars and cities (sack of Novgorod).
  • Consequences: economic ruin, weakening of the country, deterioration of the peasants' situation.
Results of the reign
  • Strengthening of autocratic power.
  • Expansion of territory, but economic crisis.
  • Dynastic crisis – murder of Tsarevich Ivan.

topics.title: Time of Troubles (1598–1613)
topics.content:
Causes
  • Dynastic crisis: extinction of the Rurik dynasty after the death of Feodor Ioannovich (1598).
  • Socio‑economic crisis: consequences of the oprichnina, Livonian War, famine of 1601–1603.
  • Discontent among various social strata.
Chronology of events
  • 1598–1605 – reign of Boris Godunov (the first elected tsar).
  • 1605–1606 – False Dmitry I (an impostor supported by Poland), his rule and death.
  • 1606–1610 – Vasily Shuisky, uprising of Ivan Bolotnikov (1606–1607).
  • 1608–1610 – False Dmitry II ("the Tushino thief"), dual power.
  • 1610 – overthrow of Shuisky, transfer of power to the Seven Boyars, invitation of Polish prince Władysław, Polish intervention.
  • 1611 – First Militia (Prokopy Lyapunov) – unsuccessful.
  • 1612 – Second Militia (Kuzma Minin, Dmitry Pozharsky), liberation of Moscow.
Zemsky Sobor of 1613

Election of a new tsar – Mikhail Feodorovich Romanov (beginning of the Romanov dynasty).

Consequences of the Time of Troubles
  • Economic ruin, human losses.
  • Strengthening of the idea of autocracy.
  • Foreign policy losses (Smolensk went to Poland).

topics.title: Russia under the first Romanovs (17th century)
topics.content:
Mikhail Feodorovich (1613–1645)
  • Restoration of the economy after the Time of Troubles.
  • Strengthening of autocracy, increasing the role of Zemsky Sobors (in the early years).
  • Treaty of Stolbovo with Sweden (1617) and Truce of Deulino with Poland (1618).
Alexei Mikhailovich (1645–1676)
  • Sobornoye Ulozhenie of 1649 – a new code of laws, final enserfment of peasants (indefinite search for runaways), formalisation of the estate structure.
  • Church schism: reforms of Patriarch Nikon (correction of books and rituals), emergence of Old Believers (Archpriest Avvakum). Confrontation between church and secular authorities.
  • Uprisings: Salt Riot (1648), Copper Riot (1662), uprising of Stepan Razin (1670–1671) – a Cossack‑peasant movement in the south.
  • Foreign policy: annexation of Left‑bank Ukraine (Pereyaslav Council, 1654), war with Poland, exploration of Siberia (Semyon Dezhnev, Khabarov).

topics.title: The era of Peter I: reforms and modernisation (1682–1725)
topics.content:
Beginning of the reign

Joint rule with his brother Ivan V under the regency of Tsarevna Sophia (1682–1689). Struggle for power, removal of Sophia.

Foreign policy
  • Azov campaigns (1695–1696) – capture of Azov, access to the Sea of Azov.
  • Grand Embassy (1697–1698) – trip to Europe to study and seek allies.
  • Great Northern War (1700–1721) with Sweden: defeat at Narva (1700), victory at Poltava (1709), naval victories at Gangut (1714) and Grengam (1720), Treaty of Nystad – access to the Baltic.
Reforms
  • State administration: establishment of the Senate (1711), collegia (1717–1721), provincial reform (1708–1710).
  • Church reform: abolition of the patriarchate, creation of the Holy Synod (1721).
  • Military reform: introduction of conscription, creation of a regular army and navy, Table of Ranks (1722).
  • Economic reform: development of manufactories, protectionism.
  • Social reform: decree on single inheritance (1714), Table of Ranks.
  • Cultural reform: opening of schools, introduction of the civil script, establishment of the Academy of Sciences (1724), construction of St. Petersburg (1703).
Proclamation of the Empire (1721)

Russia became an empire, Peter I became emperor. Significance: access to the sea, creation of a powerful army and navy, Europeanisation of the country.

Assessments

Peter I is a controversial figure: a reformer and moderniser, but at the cost of enormous efforts and sacrifices.

topics.title: Era of palace coups (1725–1762)
topics.content:
Causes
  • Lack of a clear succession order (Peter I's decree allowed the emperor to appoint his own heir).
  • The decisive role of the guard (noble regiments) in changing power.
Chronology
  • Catherine I (1725–1727) – wife of Peter I, effectively ruled by the Supreme Privy Council (Menshikov).
  • Peter II (1727–1730) – grandson of Peter I, influence of the Dolgorukovs, died of smallpox.
  • Anna Ioannovna (1730–1740) – niece of Peter I. Invited by the Supreme Privy Council under conditions limiting her power (Conditions), but tore them up. Reign relying on Courland Germans (Biron – "Bironovshchina").
  • Ivan VI (1740–1741) – infant emperor, regency first of Biron, then of his mother Anna Leopoldovna. Overthrown.
  • Elizabeth Petrovna (1741–1761) – daughter of Peter I. Return to Peter's traditions, abolition of the death penalty, foundation of Moscow University (1755). Participation in the Seven Years' War (1756–1763).
  • Peter III (1761–1762) – nephew of Elizabeth. Manifesto on the Freedom of the Nobility (freeing nobles from compulsory service). Stopped the war with Prussia, causing discontent among the guard. Overthrown by his wife.
Results

Strengthening the role of the nobility, relative stabilisation of internal political life after a series of coups.

topics.title: Reign of Catherine II. The policy of "enlightened absolutism"
topics.content:
Catherine II (1762–1796)

A German princess who came to power as a result of a coup. Ideas of the Enlightenment (correspondence with Voltaire, Diderot).

Domestic policy
  • Convocation of the Legislative Commission (1767–1768) to create a new code of laws – the work failed but revealed the sentiments of the estates.
  • Provincial reform (1775) – increase in the number of provinces, strengthening of local authority.
  • Charter to the Nobility (1785) – confirmation of all privileges, exemption from taxes and corporal punishment.
  • Charter to the Towns (1785) – division of townspeople into categories, creation of self‑government bodies.
  • Peasant war led by Yemelyan Pugachev (1773–1775) – the largest uprising of Cossacks and peasants, suppressed by government troops.
Foreign policy
  • Russo‑Turkish wars (1768–1774, 1787–1791) – annexation of Crimea (1783), access to the Black Sea, creation of the Black Sea Fleet.
  • Partitions of Poland (1772, 1793, 1795) – Russia gained Belarus, Right‑bank Ukraine, Lithuania, Courland.
  • Struggle against revolutionary France.
Development of culture and science
  • Foundation of the Hermitage, Academy of Arts.
  • Development of literature (Derzhavin, Fonvizin), journalism.
  • Emergence of private printing houses.

topics.title: Paul I (1796–1801): a controversial emperor
topics.content:
Personality and ideas

Paul I – son of Catherine II and Peter III. Antipathy toward his mother and her policies. Ideals: chivalry, order, discipline.

Domestic policy
  • Limitation of noble privileges: repeal of the Charter to the Nobility, permission of corporal punishment for nobles.
  • Decree on succession (1797) – transfer of power strictly through the male line.
  • Military reform – introduction of Prussian practices (drill, corporal punishment), which caused discontent in the army.
  • Improvement of the peasants' situation (manifesto on the three‑day corvée, prohibition of selling peasants without land).
Foreign policy
  • Participation in anti‑French coalitions (Suvorov's Italian and Swiss campaigns).
  • Break with England, rapprochement with Napoleon (plans for a campaign in India).
Conspiracy and murder

Discontent with the policy led to a conspiracy among guard officers. On the night of 11–12 March 1801, Paul was murdered in the Mikhailovsky Castle.

Contradictory assessments

Some considered him a despot, others a knight trying to restore order.

topics.title: Russia in the first quarter of the 19th century. Alexander I and the Patriotic War of 1812.
topics.content:
Alexander I (1801–1825)

Raised in a liberal spirit, he began with reforms.

Liberal initiatives
  • Unofficial Committee (Kochubey, Stroganov, Novosiltsev, Czartoryski) – preparation of reforms.
  • Establishment of ministries (1802) instead of collegia.
  • Decree on free cultivators (1803) – permission to free peasants with land.
  • Reforms of M.M. Speransky (plan of transformations, creation of the State Council in 1810).
Foreign policy before 1812
  • Participation in anti‑Napoleonic coalitions.
  • Treaty of Tilsit (1807) with France – joining the Continental blockade of England.
  • War with Sweden (1808–1809) – annexation of Finland.
Patriotic War of 1812
  • Causes: Russia's violation of the Continental blockade, Napoleon's desire for world domination.
  • Course of the war: invasion of the "Grand Army" (12 June), retreat of the Russian armies (Barclay de Tolly, Bagration), junction near Smolensk, appointment of M.I. Kutuzov as commander‑in‑chief, Battle of Borodino (26 August), council at Fili, abandonment of Moscow, Tarutino manoeuvre, partisan movement, retreat and destruction of the French army.
  • Foreign campaigns of the Russian army (1813–1814) – liberation of Europe, capture of Paris.
Congress of Vienna (1814–1815)

New order in Europe, creation of the Holy Alliance (Russia, Prussia, Austria) to fight revolutions.

Domestic policy after the war
  • Strengthening of conservative tendencies (Arakcheev, military settlements).
  • Projects for the abolition of serfdom (Novosiltsev, Arakcheev) – not implemented.
  • Contradictory personality of Alexander (mysticism, disillusionment).

topics.title: Decembrist movement (1816–1825)
topics.content:
Causes of the emergence of secret societies
  • Influence of foreign campaigns (acquaintance with European life, ideas of the Enlightenment).
  • Disappointment in the reforms of Alexander I.
  • Backwardness of serfdom and autocracy.
First organisations
  • Union of Salvation (1816–1817) – a small group, plans for regicide.
  • Union of Prosperity (1818–1821) – a broader organisation, propaganda, creation of secret boards.
Northern and Southern societies
  • Southern Society (in Ukraine) – P.I. Pestel, "Russkaya Pravda": republic, strict centralisation, separation of powers, emancipation of peasants with land.
  • Northern Society (St. Petersburg) – N.M. Muravyov, "Constitution": constitutional monarchy, federation, emancipation of peasants without land (or with a small allotment). More moderate.
Uprising of 14 December 1825

The death of Alexander I and the interregnum (Nicholas I was to take the throne). The Decembrists brought troops to the Senate Square demanding the abolition of autocracy and the introduction of a constitution. The uprising was suppressed, the leaders arrested.

Uprising of the Chernigov regiment in the south

Suppressed by government troops.

Reasons for defeat
  • Insufficient preparation, lack of unity, wait‑and‑see tactics.
  • Support of the army and the people for the new tsar.
Investigation and trial

Five were executed (Pestel, Ryleyev, Muravyov‑Apostol, Bestuzhev‑Ryumin, Kakhovsky), the rest were exiled to Siberia.

Significance of the movement
  • The first open protest against autocracy with political demands.
  • Influence on public consciousness, tradition of the liberation movement.

topics.title: Nicholas I (1825–1855): the apogee of autocracy
topics.content:
Personality of Nicholas I

A military man, pedant, convinced supporter of autocracy. His reign began with the Decembrist uprising, which determined his conservative course.

Strengthening autocracy
  • Creation of the Third Section of His Imperial Majesty's Own Chancellery (political police) and the Corps of Gendarmes.
  • Censorship statute (1826) – "cast‑iron" censorship.
  • Codification of laws (M.M. Speransky) – creation of the Complete Collection of Laws and the Digest of Laws of the Russian Empire (1832).
Financial reform (E.F. Kankrin)

Introduction of the silver ruble, financial stabilisation.

Peasant question
  • Reform of state peasants by P.D. Kiselyov (1837–1841) – improved management, creation of schools, hospitals, allocation of land to land‑poor peasants.
  • Decree on obligated peasants (1842) – permission for landowners to free peasants with land for duties (almost never used).
Public thought
  • Theory of Official Nationality (S.S. Uvarov): Orthodoxy, Autocracy, Nationality.
  • Westernisers (T.N. Granovsky, K.D. Kavelin) – Russia should follow the European path.
  • Slavophiles (A.S. Khomyakov, I.V. Kireyevsky) – a unique path, reliance on the commune and Orthodoxy.
  • Petrashevsky Circle (socialist ideas, crushed in 1849).
Foreign policy
  • Caucasian War (1817–1864) – subjugation of the highlanders of the North Caucasus.
  • Suppression of the Polish uprising (1830–1831) – abolition of the Polish constitution.
  • Russo‑Persian and Russo‑Turkish wars – expansion of influence in the Caucasus and the Balkans.
  • Crimean War (1853–1856): causes – struggle for influence in the Balkans. Course – Battle of Sinop, siege of Sevastopol. Russia's defeat (Treaty of Paris) revealed technical and economic backwardness.

topics.title: Great reforms of Alexander II (1855–1881)
topics.content:
Prerequisites for reforms
  • Defeat in the Crimean War exposed Russia's backwardness.
  • Socio‑economic development required the abolition of serfdom.
  • Peasant discontent (growth of uprisings).
Alexander II (1855–1881)

Recognised the need for transformations.

Abolition of serfdom (1861)
  • Manifesto of 19 February 1861 – proclamation of freedom.
  • Peasants received personal freedom and civil rights.
  • Land was provided for redemption (state assistance – redemption payments).
  • Until redemption, peasants were considered temporarily obliged (performed corvée or paid quitrent).
  • The size of the allotment was determined by agreement with the landowner, often peasants received "cut‑offs" (less than before).
  • Significance: creation of a free labour market, development of capitalism, but preservation of relics (commune, land scarcity).
Zemstvo (1864) and city (1870) reforms

Creation of elected bodies of local self‑government – zemstvos and city dumas (in charge of economic issues, education, medicine).

Judicial reform (1864)
  • Introduction of an independent court, transparency, adversarial proceedings (prosecutor and defence lawyer).
  • Jury trial (for criminal cases).
  • Justices of the peace for minor cases.
Military reform (1860s–1870s)
  • Introduction of universal military service (instead of conscription).
  • Shortening of service terms, rearmament, creation of military gymnasiums.
Reforms in education and press
  • New university statutes (greater autonomy).
  • Opening of primary schools, women's gymnasiums.
  • Easing of censorship (temporary rules).
Significance of the reforms

Modernisation of the country, creation of the foundations of civil society, but the reforms were half‑hearted and did not solve all problems.

topics.title: Social movement in post‑reform Russia
topics.content:
Conservative direction

M.N. Katkov, K.P. Pobedonostsev – defence of autocracy, Orthodoxy, criticism of reforms.

Liberal direction

B.N. Chicherin, K.D. Kavelin – for continuation of reforms, expansion of zemstvo rights, constitutional projects. Zemstvo movement.

Narodism (Populism)
  • Ideology: A.I. Herzen, N.G. Chernyshevsky – the idea of Russian socialism, reliance on the peasant commune.
  • Three currents:
    • Rebellious (anarchist) – M.A. Bakunin: the people are ready for rebellion, it must be raised.
    • Propagandist – P.L. Lavrov: need to go to the people, educate and prepare them for revolution.
    • Conspiratorial – P.N. Tkachev: a narrow group of revolutionaries should seize power.
  • "Going to the people" (1870s) – attempts at propaganda among the peasants, unsuccessful due to lack of understanding.
  • Organisation "Land and Liberty" (1876) – split into "Black Repartition" (G.V. Plekhanov, continuation of propaganda) and "People's Will" (A.I. Zhelyabov, S.L. Perovskaya) – terror against the tsar.
  • 1 March 1881 – assassination of Alexander II (by Narodnaya Volya terrorists).

topics.title: Counter‑reforms of Alexander III (1881–1894)
topics.content:
Alexander III

Conservative, after his father's assassination took a course to strengthen autocracy. Ideologist – K.P. Pobedonostsev.

Manifesto on the Unshakeability of Autocracy (1881)

Refusal to continue reforms.

Measures to strengthen autocracy
  • Strengthening administrative control, expansion of governors' powers.
  • Land captains (1889) – appointed from the nobility, controlled peasant self‑government.
  • New statute on zemstvos (1890) – strengthening the role of the nobility, limitation of electivity.
  • City statute (1892) – limitation of voting rights for townspeople.
  • Tightening of censorship (closure of liberal journals).
  • Policy of Russification (limitation of rights of national minorities).
Socio‑economic development
  • Completion of the industrial revolution, growth of factories, railways.
  • Labour question: factory legislation (limitation of child labour, inspection), but strikes continued (Morozov strike 1885).
  • Financial stabilisation (reforms of N.H. Bunge, I.A. Vyshnegradsky).
Foreign policy
  • Rapprochement with France (Russo‑French alliance 1891–1893) – a counterweight to the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria‑Hungary, Italy).
  • Peaceful stance in the Balkans, avoidance of conflicts.
Results

Stabilisation of the political regime, but conservation of social contradictions, postponement of urgent reforms.

topics.title: Russia at the turn of the 19th–20th centuries. Economic development and social contradictions
topics.content:
Features of Russian modernisation
  • High rates of industrial growth (1890s – industrial boom).
  • High concentration of production (large factories).
  • Active role of the state in the economy (orders, subsidies, railway construction).
  • Active inflow of foreign capital.
Reforms of S.Yu. Witte
  • Monetary reform (1897) – introduction of the gold standard, strengthening of the ruble.
  • Wine monopoly (1895) – increase in state revenues.
  • Construction of the Trans‑Siberian Railway.
  • Policy of protectionism.
Social contradictions
  • Agrarian question: land scarcity for peasants, preservation of the commune, redemption payments, backwardness of agriculture.
  • Labour question: harsh working conditions, low wages, lack of social protection, growth of strikes.
  • National movements on the outskirts (Poland, Finland, Caucasus).
Emergence of political parties
  • RSDLP (1898) – social democrats, split into Bolsheviks (Lenin) and Mensheviks (Martov).
  • Socialist Revolutionaries (PSR, 1902) – heirs of populism, terror.
  • Constitutional Democrats (Cadets, 1905) – liberals, for a constitutional monarchy.
  • Octobrists ("Union of 17 October") – moderate liberals.
Russo‑Japanese War (1904–1905)
  • Causes: clash of interests in China and Korea.
  • Course: Japanese attack on Port Arthur, sinking of the battleship "Petropavlovsk", battles of Liaoyang and Mukden, Battle of Tsushima (destruction of the Russian fleet).
  • Treaty of Portsmouth (1905): Russia ceded southern Sakhalin, the lease of Port Arthur, recognised Korea as Japan's sphere of influence. The defeat undermined the government's authority.

topics.title: Revolution of 1905–1907
topics.content:
Causes
  • Unresolved agrarian, labour, and national questions.
  • Defeat in the Russo‑Japanese War.
  • "Bloody Sunday" (9 January 1905) – shooting of a peaceful march to the Winter Palace (priest Gapon).
Course of the revolution
  • Spring‑summer 1905 – wave of strikes, peasant uprisings, creation of Soviets (Ivanovo‑Voznesensk).
  • Uprising on the battleship "Potemkin" (June 1905).
  • All‑Russian October political strike.
  • Manifesto of 17 October 1905 (Nicholas II) – granting of civil liberties, creation of a legislative State Duma.
  • December armed uprising in Moscow (suppressed).
  • Activity of the First (April–July 1906) and Second (February–June 1907) State Dumas – conflict with the government.
  • The Third of June coup (1907) – dissolution of the Second Duma and change of the electoral law (in favour of the nobility). End of the revolution.
Results
  • Creation of a parliament (State Duma), legalisation of political parties.
  • Improvement of workers' conditions (limitation of the working day, permission for trade unions).
  • Abolition of redemption payments for peasants (from 1907).
  • But the main contradictions were not resolved, leading to new revolutions.

topics.title: Stolypin agrarian reform
topics.content:
P.A. Stolypin

Prime minister in 1906–1911. His goal was to create a class of peasant‑owners as a support for the state.

Objectives of the reform
  • Destruction of the commune, enabling peasants to leave for cut‑offs (otrubs) and homesteads (khutors).
  • Increase agricultural production.
  • Relieve social tension in the countryside.
Measures
  • Decree of 9 November 1906 (law of 1910) – the right to leave the commune with land secured as private property.
  • Encouragement of peasant resettlement to Siberia, the Far East, and Central Asia (to develop new lands and reduce land shortage).
  • Activities of the Peasant Bank (loans for land purchase).
Results
  • About 25% of peasant households left the commune.
  • Growth of agricultural production, increase in grain exports.
  • Resettlement policy: some settlers returned.
  • The reform was not completed due to Stolypin's assassination (1911) and the outbreak of war.
  • Contradictory: on the one hand, progress; on the other, resistance from commune members, preservation of landlord landownership.

topics.title: Russia in the First World War (1914–1918)
topics.content:
Causes and beginning

Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand. Russia entered the war on the side of the Entente (with France and England) against Germany and Austria‑Hungary. Aims: defence of Serbia, control over the straits.

Main operations
  • 1914 – East Prussian operation (defeat of Samsonov's 2nd Army), Battle of Galicia (success against Austria‑Hungary).
  • 1915 – Great Retreat, loss of Poland, Galicia, part of the Baltic region.
  • 1916 – Brusilov breakthrough (General A.A. Brusilov) – successful offensive on the South‑Western Front, but not supported by the allies.
Impact of the war on the economy and society
  • Growth of military spending, inflation.
  • Supply problems in cities, "Rasputinism" (Grigory Rasputin's influence on the royal family), ministerial leapfrog.
  • Growth of discontent, strikes.
Decline in the authority of the government

Failures at the front, rumours of treason at the top, loss of trust in the emperor.

topics.title: February Revolution of 1917
topics.content:
Causes
  • Hardships of the war, discontent with the authorities.
  • Food crisis (bread shortages in Petrograd).
Course of events in Petrograd
  • 23 February (8 March) 1917 – start of strikes at the Putilov factory.
  • 24–25 February – mass demonstrations, clashes with police.
  • 26 February – troops go over to the side of the rebels.
  • 27 February – rebels capture the arsenal, railway stations, government buildings.
  • Creation of the Petrograd Soviet of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies and the Provisional Committee of the State Duma (M.V. Rodzyanko).
  • 2 March – abdication of Nicholas II in favour of his brother Michael (Michael also abdicated).
Dual power

Parallel existence of the Provisional Government (liberals, Cadets, Octobrists) and the Petrograd Soviet (Socialist Revolutionaries, Mensheviks).

Policy of the Provisional Government
  • Proclamation of civil liberties.
  • Preparation for a Constituent Assembly.
  • Continuation of the war (commitments to allies).
  • Postponement of agrarian reform.
Government crises
  • April Crisis (Milyukov's note on the war) – Milyukov and Guchkov resign.
  • June Crisis (failure of the offensive).
  • July Crisis (shooting of a demonstration, Lenin goes into hiding, strengthening of the Bolsheviks).
Kornilov affair

Attempt to establish a military dictatorship (August 1917) failed due to resistance from the Soviets and Bolsheviks.

topics.title: October Revolution of 1917
topics.content:
The Bolsheviks' course for an armed uprising

V.I. Lenin, returning from emigration (April 1917), put forward the "April Theses" – a course for a socialist revolution. By autumn, the Bolsheviks had gained a majority in the Soviets.

Preparation and conduct of the uprising
  • 10 October – Central Committee decision to launch an uprising.
  • Military Revolutionary Committee under the Petrograd Soviet (L.D. Trotsky).
  • On the night of 25 October (7 November), Red Guard detachments seized strategic points in Petrograd.
  • Morning of 25 October – proclamation "To the Citizens of Russia" announcing the overthrow of the Provisional Government.
  • Evening – storming of the Winter Palace, arrest of the ministers.
Second All‑Russian Congress of Soviets
  • Decree on Peace (proposal to all warring countries to conclude peace without annexations and indemnities).
  • Decree on Land (abolition of landlord ownership, nationalisation of land, transfer of land to the peasants).
  • Formation of the Council of People's Commissars (Sovnarkom) headed by Lenin.
Establishment of Soviet power locally

By spring 1918, Soviet power was established mainly in the European part of Russia (the "triumphal march").

Reasons for the Bolsheviks' victory
  • Skilful propaganda (slogans "Peace to the peoples", "Land to the peasants", "Factories to the workers").
  • Weakness of the Provisional Government.
  • Organisation and discipline of the party.

topics.title: Civil War and foreign intervention in Russia (1918–1922)
topics.content:
Causes and main opposing forces
  • The Reds – Bolsheviks, Soviet power.
  • The Whites – supporters of the old order (officers, Cossacks, part of the intelligentsia). Leaders: A.V. Kolchak, A.I. Denikin, N.N. Yudenich, P.N. Wrangel.
  • Peasant uprisings (the Greens) against the policy of "War Communism" (Makhnovshchina, Antonovshchina).
  • Intervention of the Entente countries (support for the Whites, desire to recover debts).
Beginning of the war

May 1918 – rebellion of the Czechoslovak Legion (trains with Czechs stretched from the Volga to the Far East). Creation of White governments in Siberia and the south.

Main stages
  • 1918–1919 – White offensives: Kolchak in the Urals, Denikin in the south (reaching Orel), Yudenich near Petrograd.
  • 1919–1920 – counter‑offensive of the Red Army (Trotsky – commander‑in‑chief), defeat of Kolchak, Denikin, Yudenich.
  • 1920 – Soviet‑Polish war (defeat of the Red Army near Warsaw, Treaty of Riga).
  • 1920 – defeat of Wrangel in Crimea.
  • 1921–1922 – establishment of Soviet power in the Caucasus, Central Asia, and the Far East.
Policy of "War Communism" (1918–1921)
  • Prodrazvyorstka (requisition of all surplus grain from peasants).
  • Nationalisation of all industry.
  • Prohibition of private trade.
  • Universal labour duty.
  • Rationing system.
Results and consequences
  • Huge human losses (about 10–15 million).
  • Devastation, famine, epidemics.
  • Establishment of a one‑party system, curtailment of democratic freedoms.

topics.title: New Economic Policy (NEP) 1921–1928
topics.content:
Reasons for the transition to NEP
  • Economic and political crisis: peasant uprisings (Antonovshchina), Kronstadt sailors' mutiny (March 1921).
  • Need to restore the economy.
NEP measures
  • Replacement of prodrazvyorstka with a food tax (smaller, fixed, sale of surplus allowed).
  • Permission for free trade.
  • Permission for land lease and small‑scale private ownership.
  • Denationalisation of small enterprises.
  • Monetary reform (chervonets) – stabilisation of the ruble.
  • Attraction of foreign capital (concessions).
Social and cultural changes

Rise in living standards, appearance of Nepmen (private traders), development of cooperatives. Relative freedom in culture, discussions.

Contradictions of NEP
  • Sales crises (price scissors – high prices for industrial goods, low for agricultural products).
  • Rising unemployment.
  • Ideological contradictions (private property in a socialist country).
Termination of NEP

At the end of the 1920s, a course was set for industrialisation and collectivisation, and NEP was gradually wound down.

topics.title: Formation of the USSR (1922)
topics.content:
Prerequisites for unification
  • The Soviet republics (RSFSR, Ukraine, Belarus, Transcaucasian Federation) were linked by treaties, had a common defence and economy.
  • Need for coordination of governance.
Unification projects
  • Autonomisation (I.V. Stalin): republics join the RSFSR as autonomous entities.
  • Federation (V.I. Lenin): equal republics create a union state.
Adoption of the Declaration and Treaty on the Formation of the USSR

30 December 1922 – the First Congress of Soviets of the USSR approved the formation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. Initially consisting of the RSFSR, Ukrainian SSR, Belarusian SSR, and Transcaucasian SFSR.

First Constitution of the USSR (1924)

It established the union structure, system of government, and division of powers between the centre and the republics.

topics.title: Industrialisation and collectivisation in the USSR
topics.content:
Course toward industrialisation
  • Adopted at the 14th Congress of the All‑Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks) in 1925. Aims: overcome technical and economic backwardness, create a powerful defence industry.
  • First Five‑Year Plan (1928–1932), second (1933–1937). Priority – heavy industry (metallurgy, machine building, energy).
  • Enthusiasm (Stakhanovite movement) and forced labour (use of Gulag prisoners).
  • Results: the USSR became an industrial power, but with a bias toward heavy industry; light industry and agriculture lagged behind.
Collectivisation of agriculture
  • Aims: supply the cities with food, extract funds for industrialisation, eliminate the kulaks as a class.
  • Mass creation of collective farms (kolkhozes).
  • Dekulakisation – deportation of wealthy peasants.
  • Famine of 1932–1933 (in Ukraine, the North Caucasus, the Volga region) – mass deaths.
  • Consequences: decline in agricultural production in the early years, but by the end of the 1930s the situation stabilised.

topics.title: Political system of the USSR in the 1930s. Mass repressions
topics.content:
Consolidation of Stalin's personal power

By the end of the 1920s, Stalin had become the sole leader, having crushed the opposition (Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev, Bukharin).

Constitution of 1936 ("Stalin Constitution")
  • Proclamation of the victory of socialism.
  • Entrenchment of the leading role of the All‑Union Communist Party (Bolsheviks).
  • Declaration of democratic rights and freedoms (not observed in practice).
Mass repressions
  • Trials of "enemies of the people" (1928–1930s) – fabricated cases against former oppositionists.
  • Great Terror of 1937–1938 (peak of repressions) – on charges of espionage, sabotage, anti‑Soviet activity, hundreds of thousands of people were shot or sent to camps (party members, military, intelligentsia, "national cadres").
  • The Gulag system – a network of forced labour camps.
  • Consequences: weakening of the army (repressions against command staff), destruction of entire social groups, fear in society.
Cult of personality of Stalin

Glorification of the leader in all spheres, ideologisation of all aspects of life.

topics.title: Foreign policy of the USSR in the 1920s–1930s
topics.content:
Breaking the diplomatic blockade
  • Genoa Conference (1922) – first participation of a Soviet delegation.
  • Treaty of Rapallo with Germany (1922) – establishment of diplomatic relations, mutual waiver of claims.
Policy of "appeasement" of aggressors

The USSR joins the League of Nations (1934). Course toward creating a system of collective security in Europe.

Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact (1939)
  • Non‑aggression treaty between the USSR and Germany and secret protocols on the division of spheres of influence in Eastern Europe.
  • The USSR gained a free hand in the Baltic states, Eastern Poland, Bessarabia.
Soviet‑Finnish War (1939–1940)
  • Causes: the USSR demanded to move the border away from Leningrad. Finland refused.
  • Course: heavy fighting, breach of the Mannerheim Line.
  • Result: annexation of part of Finnish territory (Karelian Isthmus), expulsion of the USSR from the League of Nations.
Annexation of Western Ukraine, Western Belarus, the Baltic states, Bessarabia

1939–1940 – these territories became part of the USSR.

topics.title: Great Patriotic War (1941–1945): initial period
topics.content:
Plan Barbarossa and the German attack

On 22 June 1941, Germany attacked the USSR without a declaration of war. Plan Barbarossa envisaged a lightning war (blitzkrieg) – the defeat of the Red Army in a few months.

Reasons for the Red Army's failures at the beginning of the war
  • Surprise of the attack.
  • Incomplete rearmament of the army.
  • Mistakes in assessing the enemy's plans.
  • Repressions among the command staff.
Organisation of resistance
  • Creation of the Headquarters of the Supreme High Command (I.V. Stalin).
  • State Defence Committee (GKO) – emergency authority.
  • Evacuation of industry to the east.
Battle of Smolensk (July–September 1941)

Delay of the German advance on Moscow.

Defence of Kyiv, Odesa, Sevastopol

Heroic resistance, but the cities were eventually abandoned.

Battle of Moscow (30 September 1941 – 20 April 1942)
  • German offensive (Operation Typhoon) – breakthrough to Moscow.
  • 5–6 December 1941 – counter‑offensive of the Red Army, defeat of the Germans near Moscow.
  • Collapse of the blitzkrieg plan, first major German defeat.

topics.title: Radical turning point in the war (1942–1943)
topics.content:
Battle of Stalingrad (17 July 1942 – 2 February 1943)
  • Defence of Stalingrad, Pavlov's House, Order No. 227 "Not a step back!".
  • Operation Uranus – encirclement of Paulus's 6th Army (November 1942).
  • Surrender of the remaining German troops (2 February 1943).
  • Significance: beginning of the radical turning point, capture of the strategic initiative.
Battle of Kursk (5 July – 23 August 1943)
  • The largest tank battle near Prokhorovka (12 July).
  • The Red Army goes on the offensive, liberation of Orel and Belgorod.
  • Final transfer of the initiative to the USSR.
Battle of the Dnieper (August–December 1943)
  • Liberation of Left‑bank Ukraine.
  • Crossing of the Dnieper, capture of bridgeheads, liberation of Kyiv (6 November 1943).

topics.title: Final stage of the war (1944–1945)
topics.content:
Ten Stalinist strikes (1944)
  • Lifting of the siege of Leningrad (January).
  • Liberation of Right‑bank Ukraine (Korsun‑Shevchenkovsky operation).
  • Liberation of Crimea, Odesa.
  • Defeat of Finland, Finland's withdrawal from the war.
  • Operation Bagration (June–August) – liberation of Belarus, the Baltic states.
  • Iasi‑Kishinev operation (liberation of Moldova, Romania's withdrawal from the war).
Opening of the second front (June 1944)

Allied landings in Normandy.

Liberation of Eastern European countries

Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia.

Vistula‑Oder operation (January–February 1945)

Reaching the Oder, liberation of Poland.

Battle of Berlin (April–May 1945)
  • Storming of the Seelow Heights, encirclement of Berlin.
  • 30 April – Hitler's suicide.
  • 2 May – surrender of the Berlin garrison.
  • Hoisting of the Victory Banner over the Reichstag (Yegorov and Kantaria).
Surrender of Germany

8–9 May 1945 – signing of the Act of Military Surrender.

Potsdam Conference (July–August 1945)

Settlement of the post‑war order in Germany, reparations, new borders.

Results and lessons of the war
  • Huge losses of the USSR (about 27 million people).
  • Devastation, restoration of the national economy.
  • Growth of the USSR's international prestige, transformation into a superpower.

topics.title: The USSR in the post‑war years (1945–1953)
topics.content:
Restoration of the national economy
  • Scale of destruction: thousands of towns and villages, factories, mines.
  • Sources of restoration: reparations from Germany, forced labour of prisoners, transfer of resources from the countryside.
  • Fourth Five‑Year Plan (1946–1950) – restoration and surpassing of pre‑war production levels.
  • Abolition of ration cards (1947), monetary reform (denomination).
Ideological campaigns
  • Struggle against cosmopolitanism ("Doctors' plot", "Leningrad affair").
  • Zhdanovshchina – campaign against Western influence in literature and art.
  • "Doctors' plot" (1952–1953) – accusation of a group of doctors of sabotage, halted after Stalin's death.
Atomic project

Creation of the atomic bomb (1949) – elimination of the US nuclear monopoly.

Beginning of the Cold War
  • Churchill's Fulton speech (1946) – announcement of the "Iron Curtain".
  • Creation of NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955).
  • Arms race.

topics.title: The Thaw: rule of N.S. Khrushchev (1953–1964)
topics.content:
Struggle for power after Stalin's death
  • Arrest and execution of L.P. Beria (1953).
  • Victory of N.S. Khrushchev over G.M. Malenkov and others.
20th Congress of the CPSU (1956)
  • Khrushchev's report on the cult of personality of Stalin – condemnation of mass repressions.
  • Beginning of de‑Stalinisation, rehabilitation of victims of repression (not all).
Economic reforms
  • Virgin lands campaign (Northern Kazakhstan, Siberia) – increase in grain sowing areas.
  • Creation of sovnarkhozes (1957) – decentralisation of industrial management.
  • Housing construction (Khrushchevka) – mass move into separate apartments.
Social policy
  • Increase in wages, pension reform (pensions for collective farmers).
  • Improvement of living standards.
Achievements in science and technology
  • Launch of the first artificial Earth satellite (1957).
  • First human space flight (Yuri Gagarin, 1961).
Foreign policy
  • Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) – confrontation with the US over the placement of Soviet missiles on Cuba, nearly leading to nuclear war.
  • Berlin Crisis (1961) – construction of the Berlin Wall.
  • Policy of peaceful coexistence, but also support for national liberation movements.
Khrushchev's resignation (1964)

Dissatisfaction with reforms and voluntarism; he was removed from office.

topics.title: Era of Stagnation: L.I. Brezhnev (1964–1982)
topics.content:
Coming to power

L.I. Brezhnev became First Secretary of the CPSU Central Committee (General Secretary). A.N. Kosygin (Chairman of the Council of Ministers) and others came with him.

Economic reform of 1965 (Kosygin reform)
  • Strengthening of cost accounting, reduction of planned targets, increasing the role of profit.
  • The first years gave a positive effect, but then the reform was curtailed due to resistance from the party apparatus.
Increasing stagnation
  • Decline in economic growth rates (the extensive path was exhausted).
  • Fuel and raw material dependence (oil and gas).
  • Shortage of goods, queues.
  • Shadow economy.
Constitution of 1977

Proclamation of "developed socialism", entrenchment of the leading role of the CPSU.

Foreign policy
  • Détente – SALT I (1972), SALT II (1979) treaties on the limitation of strategic arms.
  • Helsinki Accords (1975) – recognition of post‑war borders in Europe, cooperation in the humanitarian sphere.
  • Invasion of Afghanistan (1979) – end of détente, exacerbation of relations with the West.
Dissident movement

A.D. Sakharov, A.I. Solzhenitsyn and others – protests for human rights, freedom of speech, against totalitarianism. Repression by the authorities.

topics.title: Perestroika: M.S. Gorbachev (1985–1991)
topics.content:
Prerequisites for perestroika

Growth of crisis phenomena in the economy, lagging behind the West, falling productivity, arms race.

Course toward acceleration (1985)

Attempts to increase the pace of development through scientific and technical progress and discipline (anti‑alcohol campaign – led to budget losses).

Policy of glasnost

Easing of censorship, publication of previously forbidden works, discussions about the past and present. Growth of public activism.

Economic reforms
  • Law on State Enterprise (1987) – expansion of independence, but without price reform.
  • Authorisation of cooperatives (1988) – beginning of private entrepreneurship.
  • Transition to market relations, but inconsistently, leading to shortages and crisis.
Political reform
  • Introduction of the post of President of the USSR (1990), election of Gorbachev.
  • Congress of People's Deputies – new bodies of power, first alternative elections.
New thinking in foreign policy
  • Withdrawal of troops from Afghanistan (1989).
  • German reunification (1990).
  • End of the Cold War, arms reduction.
Growth of national movements, parade of sovereignties

The Baltic states, Ukraine, Georgia and other republics proclaim independence or sovereignty. Centrifugal tendencies.

August Coup (1991)

Attempt by conservative forces (GKChP) to preserve the USSR, arrest of Gorbachev in Foros, deployment of troops in Moscow. Failed due to resistance led by B.N. Yeltsin.

Collapse of the USSR

8 December 1991 – Belavezha Accords (Russia, Ukraine, Belarus) on the creation of the CIS and the end of the USSR. 25 December 1991 – Gorbachev's resignation.

topics.title: Russian Federation in the 1990s
topics.content:
Establishment of a new statehood
  • President B.N. Yeltsin (elected in 1991, re‑elected in 1996).
  • Course toward market reforms.
Economic reforms
  • Shock therapy: price liberalisation (January 1992), hyperinflation, devaluation of savings.
  • Privatisation (voucher, then monetary) – emergence of a class of owners, but also criticism for unfairness.
  • Decline in production, rise in unemployment, social stratification.
Constitutional crisis of 1993
  • Confrontation between the president and the Supreme Soviet.
  • 3–4 October 1993 – shelling of the parliament (White House) by troops.
  • 12 December 1993 – adoption of a new constitution (presidential republic), elections to the Federal Assembly.
Chechen wars
  • 1994–1996 – first Chechen war (unsuccessful, heavy losses).
  • 1999–2009 – second Chechen war, restoration of control over the republic.
Default of 1998

Economic crisis, default on domestic obligations, sharp devaluation of the ruble, then some import substitution growth.

Foreign policy

Search for a place in the world, relations with the West (joining the Council of Europe), problems with NATO (eastward expansion).

topics.title: Modern Russia: the presidencies of V.V. Putin and D.A. Medvedev
topics.content:
V.V. Putin's rise to power

31 December 1999 – B.N. Yeltsin resigned, acting president V.V. Putin. Victory in the 2000 elections.

Strengthening the power vertical
  • Creation of federal districts, reform of the Federation Council.
  • Unification of legislation, fight against separatism.
  • Limitation of governors' powers.
Economic growth in the 2000s
  • Favourable external economic conditions (high oil prices).
  • Increase in GDP, reduction of inflation.
  • Social programmes (national projects, maternity capital).
Foreign policy
  • Concept of a multipolar world.
  • Relations with the US and the EU (sometimes rapprochement, sometimes cooling).
  • Conflict with Georgia (2008) – recognition of independence of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.
  • Conflict with Ukraine (2014) – annexation of Crimea, support for Donbas, Western sanctions.
  • Participation in the military operation in Syria (since 2015).
Presidency of D.A. Medvedev (2008–2012)
  • Modernisation, innovations.
  • Law increasing the presidential term to 6 years.
Putin's return to the presidency (2012)

New socio‑economic challenges, protest actions (2011–2012).

Amendments to the Constitution of 2020

Expansion of presidential powers, zeroing of terms for the current president.

topics.title: Russian culture: from antiquity to the present day
topics.content:
Culture of Ancient Rus
  • Icon painting: Theophanes the Greek, Andrei Rublev ("Trinity").
  • Chronicle writing: Nestor's "Primary Chronicle".
  • Architecture: St. Sophia Cathedrals in Kyiv and Novgorod, Church of the Intercession on the Nerl.
Culture of the Moscow Tsardom (14th–17th centuries)
  • Icon painting: Dionysius (frescoes of the Ferapontov Monastery).
  • Architecture: Moscow Kremlin, tent‑roof architecture (St. Basil's Cathedral).
  • Literature: lives of saints, Afanasy Nikitin's "Journey Beyond Three Seas".
18th century: Europeanisation
  • Peter's reforms: introduction of the civil script, opening of schools, Kunstkamera.
  • Architecture: baroque (V.V. Rastrelli – Winter Palace), classicism.
  • Literature: M.V. Lomonosov, G.R. Derzhavin, D.I. Fonvizin.
19th century – the "Golden Age" of Russian culture
  • Literature: A.S. Pushkin, M.Yu. Lermontov, N.V. Gogol, I.S. Turgenev, L.N. Tolstoy, F.M. Dostoevsky, A.P. Chekhov.
  • Music: M.I. Glinka, P.I. Tchaikovsky, "The Mighty Handful".
  • Painting: K.P. Bryullov, A.A. Ivanov, the Wanderers (I.E. Repin, V.I. Surikov, V.G. Perov).
  • Architecture: Empire style, Russian‑Byzantine style (Cathedral of Christ the Saviour).
"Silver Age" (late 19th – early 20th century)
  • Poetry: symbolism (A.A. Blok, A. Bely), acmeism (N.S. Gumilyov, A.A. Akhmatova), futurism (V.V. Mayakovsky).
  • Prose: I.A. Bunin, A.I. Kuprin, L.N. Andreyev.
  • Painting: "World of Art" (A.N. Benois, K.A. Somov), avant‑garde (V.V. Kandinsky, K.S. Malevich).
  • Theatre: K.S. Stanislavsky, V.I. Nemirovich‑Danchenko (Moscow Art Theatre).
Soviet culture
  • 1920s: avant‑garde (constructivism), flourishing of cinema (S.M. Eisenstein).
  • 1930s–1950s: socialist realism (literature – M. Gorky, M.A. Sholokhov; painting – A.A. Deineka; architecture – Stalinist Empire style).
  • Culture during the war (agitprop brigades, posters).
  • The Thaw (1960s) – the "Sixtiers", cinema (A.A. Tarkovsky), poetry (Y.A. Yevtushenko).
  • Dissident art (I.A. Brodsky, A.D. Sakharov).
  • 1970s–1980s: bard song (V.S. Vysotsky), theatre (G.A. Tovstonogov).
Post‑Soviet culture

Diversity of styles, integration into world culture, development of mass culture, new technologies, the internet.
